content: The subversion case against the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, and the 24-day trial of the two who pleaded not guilty — Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung — will reach its verdict on Friday, August 21. Former vice-chairperson of the Alliance, Chow Hang-tung, represented herself in this case as a barrister. In prison, without access to a computer or the internet, she wrote out hundreds of pages of submissions by hand. At her application, the court played in full two years' worth of candlelight vigil recordings for the June 4 anniversary, recreating candle after candle in Victoria Park, as well as the testimony of June 4 eyewitnesses. "Well, I am the last defendant, and also the last vice-chairperson of the first defendant, the Alliance... I am 41 years old now, a barrister, and I don't really have much of a simple background." Chow Hang-tung smiled as she began. Over six days of giving evidence, she frequently smiled, but also broke down in tears several times. What does the June 4 vigil, and "ending one-party dictatorship," mean to Chow Hang-tung? What was her "intent"? In this podcast episode, we continue to take readers to the courtroom, using audio reenactment to recreate Chow Hang-tung's testimony, as well as the questioning from the judge and the prosecution. Recap: Audio reenactment — Lee Cheuk-yan's testimony: "In my heart there is no hostility, only love" Related coverage of the Hong Kong Alliance case
